clinicalPearls: An autosomal recessive hypomyelinating leukodystrophy caused by variants in GJC2, which encodes the gap junction protein connexin 47
It closely resembles X-linked Pelizaeus-Merzbacher disease (caused by PLP1) both clinically and radiologically, but follows autosomal recessive inheritance and can affect either sex
Presentation is usually in early infancy with nystagmus and hypotonia, evolving into spasticity, cerebellar ataxia, dysarthria and delayed or limited motor development
Some children never achieve independent walking, while others follow a milder course, reflecting the range of GJC2 variants
MRI shows diffuse hypomyelination with a persistently immature myelin pattern that does not progress normally with age
GJC2 testing is appropriate once PLP1-related Pelizaeus-Merzbacher disease has been considered or excluded, particularly when inheritance appears recessive or a girl is affected
There is no specific treatment, so care is supportive and multidisciplinary, with management of spasticity, physiotherapy, communication support and nutrition
reference.pathophysiology: Pelizaeus-Merzbacher-like disease is caused by biallelic variants in GJC2, encoding connexin 47, a gap junction protein expressed by oligodendrocytes. Connexin 47 forms channels between oligodendrocytes and between oligodendrocytes and astrocytes that are essential for ionic and metabolic coupling in the white matter. Loss of functional connexin 47 disrupts this glial network, impairing the ability of oligodendrocytes to establish and maintain normal myelin. The result is a hypomyelinating leukodystrophy that phenotypically overlaps with the more common PLP1-related disease, in which a different oligodendrocyte protein is affected.
additionalDifferentials: AIMP1-related and other genetic hypomyelinating leukodystrophies
Fucosidosis and storage disorders presenting with hypomyelination
additionalInvestigations: Brain MRI to demonstrate diffuse hypomyelination and to assess its pattern and stability over time
PLP1 analysis (including dosage) to address the main differential before or alongside GJC2 testing
GJC2 sequencing, with a hypomyelinating leukodystrophy panel or exome if negative
Visual evoked potentials and ophthalmology review given the early nystagmus
Nerve conduction studies to help distinguish central from peripheral involvement
Developmental and physiotherapy assessment to plan supportive care
redFlags: Failure to establish head control or feeding difficulty in a severely affected infant
Progressive respiratory compromise from bulbar and truncal weakness
Escalating spasticity or dystonia causing pain and contractures
Unexpected rapid regression prompting reconsideration of the diagnosis
reference.prognosis: The prognosis of Pelizaeus-Merzbacher-like disease spans a spectrum: severely affected children may never walk and have significant lifelong disability, whereas milder cases achieve more motor skills and a slower course. As with PLP1-related disease, many patients survive into adulthood with supportive care, and outcome depends largely on the severity of motor and bulbar involvement.
pitfalls: Testing only PLP1 and stopping when it is negative, thereby missing GJC2-related disease
Discounting the diagnosis in an affected girl because Pelizaeus-Merzbacher disease is X-linked
Mistaking hypomyelination for delayed myelination without appropriate follow-up imaging
Attributing the picture to hypoxic-ischaemic injury or cerebral palsy
Not offering autosomal recessive genetic counselling to the family
references: Bradley and Daroff's Neurology in Clinical Practice
management: Manage spasticity with physiotherapy, antispasticity medication such as baclofen, botulinum toxin and orthoses
Support feeding and nutrition and treat the consequences of dysarthria and dysphagia, using gastrostomy when needed
Provide respiratory care and manage recurrent aspiration
Deliver physiotherapy and occupational therapy for the cerebellar ataxia and delayed motor development, with mobility and communication aids
Coordinate multidisciplinary neurology and rehabilitation follow-up, as no disease-specific therapy exists for this hypomyelinating leukodystrophy
Offer genetic counselling for autosomal recessive inheritance, noting either sex may be affected, with carrier and prenatal testing for families
